title: Pitch (Longitudinal) Control

intro.en: Rev 1 — narration from the recording, cleaned ("all-flying the tail" → all-flying tail, "at tail / AT tail" → T-tail, "off CG" → aft CG, "incident(s)" → incidence, "gloing" → g-loading, "rotational flare" → rotation or flare, "your / y / ys / yoring / ying" → yaw / yaws / yawing, "weather vein" → weathervane, "aerons" → ailerons, "wing route" → wing root, "role" → roll, "sid slip" → sideslip, "fries / fry ailerons" → Frise ailerons, "crossoupling" → cross-coupling, "flap erons" → flaperons, "C." → see, "antibbalance" → anti-balance, "PO" → PIO, "control field" → control feel). Before teaching: (1) page 7 says a forward CG "shortens the distance to the elevator" and that a "shorter moment arm reduces the pitching moment generated by the elevator" — WRONG. Moving the CG forward LENGTHENS the tail arm. The real problem is that the nose-down moment (weight ahead of the lift) becomes larger, so the tail needs a bigger download and more up-elevator; at low speed you can run out of elevator authority for rotation and flare; (2) page 11 example: "rolling left with LEFT aileron down creates drag on the left wing, yawing the aircraft right" — WRONG. Rolling left, the RIGHT aileron goes down; the extra drag on the right wing yaws the nose right (adverse yaw). The recording on page 12 states it correctly; (3) page 19: "internal balance" is shown and narrated as internal WEIGHTS that move the surface CG forward — that is MASS balance (anti-flutter, page 6 of 081 06 01 01), not aerodynamic internal balance. Internal (aerodynamic) balance is a balance panel or nose section inside the wing, ahead of the hinge, sealed to the wing so that the pressure difference between upper and lower surfaces acts on it and assists movement; (4) page 20: the balance tab and anti-balance tab do not change "control surface inertia" — they change the HINGE MOMENT (stick force). The servo tab is not "connected directly to a servo motor … used in autopilots or fly-by-wire" — the pilot's controls move only the tab; the main surface floats and is driven by the tab's aerodynamic force (autopilot servo-motors are a different item); (5) the recording on page 23 says the spring tab produces "more resistance … depending on design" — a spring tab ASSISTS (acts as a balance tab) increasingly as speed rises; (6) fleet links: C172S — conventional tail with elevator and trim tab; Piper-style stabilators carry an anti-balance (anti-servo) tab (page 22 photo); DA42 HS-NAS — T-tail (page 5) and twin-engine asymmetric case (page 13): VMCA and the 2–5° bank toward the live engine are AFM items (SME); (7) remove all "[cite: nn]" artefacts in Canva.

pages.t: Pitch (longitudinal) control: overview
pages.on: "PITCH (LONGITUDINAL) CONTROL" — working principles and functions of elevator and all-flying tail systems; C172 axes image.
pages.en: Pitch, or longitudinal, control is managed mainly by the elevator or by an all-flying tail (stabilator). The key idea is simple: these surfaces create a force on the tail that produces a pitching moment about the centre of gravity. The tailplane load changes across the speed range. At low speeds, such as take-off and landing, the tailplane commonly has to produce a downward load to counter nose-down pitching tendencies and to give the pilot enough pitch authority — you will often see the elevator deflected upward to increase the tail download and keep the aircraft controllable at low dynamic pressure. At high speeds the tailplane may carry either an upward or a downward load, depending on the design and the trim condition, because the aerodynamic forces are larger and only small deflections are needed for manoeuvring. Tail loads change rapidly as the pilot commands pitch changes, and those loads can become significant because both angle of attack and g-loading change. A major factor in tailplane effectiveness is downwash. The wing deflects the airflow downward; that downwash reaches the tailplane and reduces the tail's effective angle of attack, which can reduce tail lift and influence pitch stability. Designers reduce downwash effects with configurations such as the T-tail, which places the tailplane higher and often in cleaner airflow, and with stabiliser trim, which allows the tailplane incidence to be adjusted to provide the required balancing moment efficiently. CG location also matters. With an aft CG the aircraft becomes more pitch-sensitive, so smaller elevator deflections give a given response. With a forward CG the aircraft is less sensitive and needs larger elevator deflections, and at the forward limit the available elevator authority can run out, making pitch-up difficult at low speed and increasing the required angle of attack, which raises the stall speed.

pages.t: Loads on the tailplane across speed ranges
pages.on: Infographic: (1) low speeds — download, elevator up; (2) high speeds (cruise) — up or down load; (3) manoeuvring — rapid, dynamic load changes.
pages.en: Tailplane loads change significantly with speed and flight condition, because the tail's job is to provide the balancing pitching moment about the centre of gravity. As dynamic pressure changes and as pitch demands change, the stabiliser and elevator must produce different amounts — and sometimes different directions — of force. At low speeds, especially during take-off and landing, dynamic pressure is relatively low, so the control surfaces are less effective for a given deflection. At the same time the aircraft often needs a strong balancing moment to manage pitch attitude and to rotate or flare. In many conventional designs the tailplane provides a downward load to counter the aircraft's nose-down pitching tendency. To increase that download at low speed the pilot uses up-elevator, which pushes the tail down and pitches the nose up. This is why elevator deflection is more noticeable at low speed: more deflection is needed for the same pitching effect. At high speeds, such as cruise, the aerodynamic forces are much larger. Because the airflow is stronger, the tail can produce the required balancing moment with relatively small deflections, and depending on design and trim the tailplane may carry either a downward or an upward load. What matters is not the direction by itself but that the tail produces the correct moment to balance the wing and fuselage pitching moments at that speed, power setting and CG position. During manoeuvring, tailplane loads can change rapidly. Any pitch manoeuvre — pulling up, pushing over, entering or recovering from a climb or descent — needs changes in angle of attack and often in g-loading, which force the tail to respond dynamically, with quick increases or decreases in aerodynamic load as the elevator moves and the stabiliser's effective angle of attack changes. That is why pitch manoeuvres demand smooth control: the tail is seeing fast-changing loads, and the aircraft's response can be immediate, especially at higher speeds.

pages.t: Downwash effects on aircraft tailplane
pages.on: Infographic: (1) wing generates downwash, (2) tailplane encounters it, (3) reduced tail angle of attack, (4) impact on lift and pitch stability.
pages.en: The wing does not just create lift; it also changes the airflow behind it. As the wing produces lift it generates downwash — the airflow is deflected downward as it passes over and behind the wing. That downwash travels aft, and the tailplane meets it. From the tail's point of view the oncoming airflow is now angled downward rather than straight. The key result is that the tailplane's effective angle of attack is reduced: even if the tailplane's geometric angle has not changed, the relative wind it sees has, so the tail is working at a lower effective angle of attack. When the effective angle of attack changes, the tailplane's ability to produce its required aerodynamic force — upward or downward, depending on configuration — changes as well. That directly affects the lift generated at the tail and therefore the pitching-moment balance about the CG. In practical terms, downwash influences how much tail force is available for trimming and how strongly the aircraft responds in pitch, because pitch stability depends on predictable, consistent restoring moments. Downwash also affects longitudinal stability. Changes in wing lift, flap setting or angle of attack change the strength of the downwash, which alters tail effectiveness. That is why an aircraft can feel different in pitch as its configuration changes: the wing is changing the airflow environment of the tailplane, and the tail must then produce a different force to keep the same trim condition.

pages.t: Mitigation strategies for tailplane downwash effects
pages.on: Infographic: (1) T-tail configuration, (2) stabiliser trim (adjustable tailplane angle of attack); critical role in flight.
pages.en: Downwash can reduce the tailplane's effective angle of attack and change how much balancing force the tail can produce, so designers and pilots use a couple of key strategies to reduce its impact and keep pitch control consistent. One strategy is the T-tail configuration. By mounting the tailplane on top of the fin, the tail is placed higher and, in many cases, further away from the strongest part of the wing downwash and the propeller slipstream. The benefit is more consistent airflow at the tail across normal flight conditions, which helps keep a more predictable effective angle of attack and improves pitch-control feel. The trade-off is that a T-tail can be more sensitive at very high angles of attack, when the tail can be immersed in the wake of a stalled wing; but as a downwash-mitigation method in normal flight it is a common and effective design solution. The second strategy is stabiliser trim, meaning the tailplane incidence — the tail setting — can be adjusted. Instead of relying only on elevator deflection to create the required tail force, the pilot or an aircraft system adjusts the stabiliser, so the tailplane works at a more suitable angle of attack for the current speed, configuration and power setting. This helps counteract changes caused by downwash and reduces the continuous elevator input needed to stay in equilibrium. In practical terms, stabiliser trim improves efficiency and handling because the aircraft keeps the correct pitching-moment balance with less drag and less control pressure. Together, placing the tail in cleaner airflow with a T-tail and adjusting tailplane incidence with stabiliser trim are two effective ways to keep pitch control stable and predictable despite changing downwash.

pages.t: Location of centre of gravity (CG) and elevator deflection
pages.on: Infographic: forward CG (less pitch-sensitive, larger elevator deflections) vs aft CG (more pitch-sensitive, smaller deflections); stability vs manoeuvrability.
pages.en: The position of the centre of gravity changes how much leverage the elevator and tailplane have over the aircraft's pitching moment, so it directly changes pitch sensitivity and the elevator deflection needed for the same result. With an aft CG the aircraft becomes more pitch-sensitive. Because the CG is closer to the neutral point, the aircraft has less natural restoring tendency in pitch, and a smaller tail force can create a noticeable change in pitching moment. In practice, smaller elevator deflections give the same pitch response; the aircraft may feel lighter and more responsive in pitch, but it also becomes easier to over-control, and pitch oscillations can develop if inputs are abrupt. With a forward CG the aircraft is less pitch-sensitive. The tail must produce a larger balancing moment to trim the aircraft, and the elevator has to work harder to change that moment. As a result the pilot needs larger elevator deflections for the same pitch change; control forces feel heavier and pitch changes feel more deliberate. This generally increases stability, but it can also reduce the pitch authority available at low speed, such as during rotation or the flare, because more elevator is needed just when aerodynamic effectiveness is reduced. The practical takeaway: aft CG means more responsive, smaller inputs; forward CG means more stable, larger inputs. Pilots must anticipate this across loading conditions so that pitch control stays smooth and precise in every phase of flight.

pages.t: Effect of forward CG limit on pitch control and performance
pages.on: Infographic: (1) forward CG position, (2) reduced elevator effectiveness — "shorter moment arm", (3) difficulty pitching up at low speed, (4) increased stall speed.
pages.en: At the forward CG limit, pitch control becomes more demanding because the tail and elevator have to work harder to produce the pitching moments needed for rotation, flare and manoeuvring. The first effect is that the elevator's available authority is used up sooner. With the CG further forward, the weight acting ahead of the lift creates a stronger nose-down moment that the tail must balance. Note that the tail arm actually becomes slightly longer, not shorter — the problem is the size of the nose-down moment, not the lever. The elevator must therefore generate a larger aerodynamic force to produce the same pitch-up moment, and at low speed the elevator has less airflow and therefore less authority. In practical terms you may run out of elevator before reaching the pitch attitude you want — most noticeably during the take-off rotation and the landing flare, when you need a strong pitch-up command at relatively low airspeed. This leads directly to difficulty pitching up, especially in low-speed phases: even with the elevator at or near full deflection, the aircraft may respond slowly or may not reach the desired nose-up attitude. That is why forward CG limits are tightly controlled — they protect against situations where the aircraft cannot rotate or cannot flare adequately. A forward CG also tends to increase the stall speed. With the CG forward, the tail usually produces more download to balance the nose-down moment, so the wing must produce extra lift to support both the aircraft weight and the tail download. Producing more lift at a given speed needs a higher angle of attack, so the aircraft reaches the critical angle of attack sooner, which effectively raises the stall speed. The pilot takeaway: at the forward CG limit expect heavier pitch control, more elevator required and less margin at low speed. The safest approach is disciplined speed control and planning, because pitch-up authority is reduced right when you need it most.

pages.t: Yaw control overview: the rudder's role in directional control
pages.on: Infographic: (1) location — rudder on the fin, (2) operation — right/left pedal, (3) function — yawing motion, directional stability.
pages.en: Yaw control is managed mainly by the rudder, the movable control surface attached to the vertical stabiliser. Its job is to control the aircraft's directional motion — yaw — and to help keep the aircraft aligned with the airflow for coordinated flight. The rudder works by creating a side force on the tail. When you press the right rudder pedal, the rudder deflects to the right; the airflow striking the deflected rudder pushes the tail to the left, which yaws the nose to the right. Pressing the left pedal does the opposite: the rudder deflects left, the tail is pushed right, and the nose yaws left. Operationally, the rudder is used for three main purposes. First, directional control: keeping the aircraft tracking straight on the runway during take-off and landing, and controlling heading changes when needed. Second, coordination in turns: countering adverse yaw and keeping the aircraft from slipping or skidding, which you monitor with the ball. Third, it supports directional stability by helping the aircraft realign with the relative wind after disturbances, especially in turbulence. In short, the rudder is mounted on the vertical stabiliser, it yaws the aircraft by pushing the tail sideways, and it is essential for keeping the aircraft coordinated, stable and accurately pointed where you want it to go.

pages.t: Rudder functionality: the direct correlation to yaw control
pages.on: Infographic: (1) rudder deflection, (2) yawing moment, (3) yaw rate; greater deflection → larger yawing moment → faster yaw rate.
pages.en: Rudder control follows a simple cause-and-effect chain: deflection creates a yawing moment, and that yawing moment produces a yaw rate. It starts with rudder deflection: the pilot presses a pedal and the rudder moves into the airflow. That deflection changes the rudder's aerodynamic force, creating a sideways force on the tail. The tail force produces a yawing moment about the aircraft's centre of gravity. The greater the rudder deflection, the greater the side force on the tail and the larger the yawing moment available to rotate the aircraft. The result is yaw rate: the aircraft starts rotating about its normal (vertical) axis, swinging the nose left or right. In general, more rudder deflection produces a faster yaw rate, meaning the nose turns more quickly. In practice the response also depends on airspeed. At higher speed the rudder is more effective because dynamic pressure is higher, so small deflections can produce significant yawing moments. At lower speed the rudder produces less force for the same deflection, so the response is weaker and may need larger inputs. But the core relationship stays the same: bigger rudder input, bigger yawing moment, faster yaw rate.

pages.t: Yawing moments and sideslip effects
pages.on: Infographic: (1) sideslip and lateral force on the fin creating a yawing moment, (2) weathercock stability — yaws the aircraft into the relative wind.
pages.en: A sideslip occurs when the aircraft is not aligned with the relative wind, so the airflow strikes the fuselage from the side. In that condition the vertical stabiliser and rudder experience a sideways aerodynamic force. Because this force acts behind the centre of gravity, it creates a yawing moment, and that yawing moment naturally turns the aircraft's nose toward the oncoming airflow. As the nose yaws into the relative wind, the sideslip is reduced. This self-correcting behaviour is called weathercock stability, and it explains why the vertical tail is essential for directional stability: it produces the restoring yawing moment that helps the aircraft realign with the airflow after a disturbance. It is also useful to know that this effect can be more noticeable on larger aircraft. With a bigger fin and more side area exposed to the airflow, the weathervane tendency is stronger, so when a sideslip develops a large aircraft can show a more pronounced natural tendency for the heading to swing back toward the relative wind, even before the pilot makes a large rudder input.
pages.th: Sideslip เกิดเมื่อเครื่องไม่อยู่แนวเดียวกับลมสัมพัทธ์ กระแสอากาศจึงปะทะลำตัวจากด้านข้าง ในสภาพนั้นแพนหางดิ่งและ rudder จะรับแรงอากาศพลศาสตร์ด้านข้าง เพราะแรงนี้อยู่หลังจุดศูนย์ถ่วง จึงเกิดโมเมนต์ yaw และโมเมนต์ yaw นั้นหมุนหัวเครื่องเข้าหากระแสอากาศที่เข้ามาโดยธรรมชาติ เมื่อหัวหันเข้าหาลมสัมพัทธ์ sideslip ก็ลดลง พฤติกรรมแก้ตัวเองนี้เรียกว่า weathercock stability ซึ่งอธิบายว่าทำไมแพนหางดิ่งจำเป็นต่อเสถียรภาพทางทิศ มันสร้างโมเมนต์ yaw คืนตัวที่ช่วยให้เครื่องกลับมาอยู่แนวกระแสอากาศหลังถูกรบกวน ควรรู้ด้วยว่าผลนี้อาจเห็นชัดขึ้นในเครื่องขนาดใหญ่ ครีบหางที่ใหญ่และพื้นที่ด้านข้างที่สัมผัสกระแสอากาศมากทำให้แนวโน้มแบบกังหันลมแรงขึ้น เมื่อเกิด sideslip เครื่องใหญ่อาจมีแนวโน้มให้ heading เหวี่ยงกลับเข้าหาลมสัมพัทธ์ชัดเจนขึ้น แม้ก่อนนักบินจะใช้ rudder มาก

pages.t: Roll (lateral) control: understanding ailerons and aircraft manoeuvring
pages.on: Infographic: (1) aileron location, (2) differential deflection, (3) rolling moment, (4) critical role in flight.
pages.en: Roll, or lateral, control is achieved mainly with the ailerons, on the outer trailing edges of the wings. Their purpose is to create a controlled rolling moment about the longitudinal axis, so the pilot can bank left or right. When the pilot moves the control wheel or stick, the ailerons move differentially. The aileron on one wing deflects upward, which reduces camber and reduces lift on that wing. At the same time the aileron on the other wing deflects downward, increasing camber and increasing lift on that wing. This lift difference between the two wings produces a rolling moment, and the aircraft banks toward the wing with reduced lift (the up-aileron side) and away from the wing with increased lift. In practice, aileron use must be coordinated with rudder, because changing lift also changes drag. The wing with the down-going aileron typically produces more lift but also more drag, which can pull the nose slightly in the opposite direction to the intended turn. This is why smooth roll control involves not only aileron input but also the correct rudder input, to keep the aircraft coordinated and the ball centred. Used precisely, the ailerons let pilots establish and adjust bank angle smoothly, making them essential for turns, turbulence corrections, and accurate lateral control throughout the flight.

pages.t: Aileron functioning: control, effects and safety mechanisms
pages.on: Infographic: (1) adverse yaw — example "rolling left with left aileron down … yawing right", (2) inboard and outboard ailerons, (3) outboard-aileron lockout.
pages.en: Ailerons create roll by changing the lift on each wing, but they also introduce side effects, especially adverse yaw — and that is why some aircraft use different aileron arrangements for different speed ranges. Adverse yaw happens because the wing with the down-going aileron produces more lift but also more drag, and that extra drag pulls the nose opposite to the intended roll. For example, if you roll left, the left aileron deflects up and the right aileron deflects down. The right wing now has more lift and more drag, so the nose tends to yaw right while you are trying to bank left. The practical pilot response is coordinated rudder: add rudder in the direction of the turn to keep the aircraft aligned and the ball centred. To optimise roll control across the speed envelope, designers may use inboard and outboard ailerons. Inboard ailerons are closer to the wing root and are used at all speeds, including high speed. Outboard ailerons are nearer the wing tip and are most useful at low speed, where dynamic pressure is low and the longer arm gives more rolling moment — during approach and landing, for example. At high dynamic pressure, however, outboard ailerons carry an important risk: the wing can twist under the aerodynamic load of the aileron. If the twist changes the wing's angle of attack in the wrong direction, the aileron input becomes less effective or, in extreme cases, produces roll in the opposite direction — aileron reversal. That is why some aircraft have an outboard-aileron lockout: as speed increases, the system locks the outboard ailerons, preventing reversal caused by wing twist, and the aircraft then relies on the inboard ailerons and roll spoilers for safe, predictable roll response at high speed. So the big picture: ailerons control roll; adverse yaw must be managed with coordination; and inboard/outboard aileron systems with lockouts keep roll control effective and safe across the speed range.

pages.t: Aileron use in various flight conditions
pages.on: Infographic: (1) normal flight, (2) sideslip, (3) crosswind landings, (4) horizontal turns, (5) one engine out.
pages.en: Ailerons are the primary control for bank and roll, and you use them differently depending on the situation, to keep the aircraft stable, coordinated and on the desired flight path. In normal flight, ailerons keep the wings level and establish the bank angle needed to start a turn. Once the desired bank is set, aileron pressure is reduced and you make small corrections to hold the attitude against turbulence and any rolling tendency. In a sideslip, aileron and rudder are used together: aileron controls the bank angle while rudder controls yaw to align the aircraft as required — for example the fuselage with the runway — and the slip is deliberate, so here the ball is not centred. In crosswind landings, ailerons counter the crosswind's rolling tendency and help manage drift. As you transition to the landing you typically hold aileron into the wind to keep the upwind wing from lifting, while rudder keeps the aircraft aligned with the runway. Aileron becomes more important as speed decreases, because the aircraft is more easily affected by gusts and rolling moments. In level turns, ailerons establish and maintain the bank, but they are part of a coordinated control set: elevator maintains altitude by increasing lift, and rudder prevents adverse yaw and keeps the turn coordinated. Ailerons set the shape of the turn, but the other controls keep it stable. With one engine out in multi-engine flight, ailerons help balance the aircraft against asymmetric forces. Rudder counters the yaw toward the dead engine, and aileron is used as needed to control bank, often holding a small bank toward the operating engine for best control and performance. Here the ailerons prevent an unwanted roll and help maintain a stable, controllable attitude, while directional control is managed with rudder. Overall, ailerons are not just for turning — they are a constant tool for roll balance, coordination and stability in nearly every phase of flight.

pages.t: Aircraft roll rate factors and related concepts
pages.on: Infographic: (1) roll rate definition (deg/s), (2) factors: aileron design, wingspan, airspeed, dihedral, moment of inertia, (3) flaperons, (4) aileron droop.
pages.en: Roll rate is the speed at which the bank angle changes — essentially, how quickly the aircraft can roll from one bank angle to another. A higher roll rate means the aircraft responds more quickly to lateral control inputs; a lower roll rate feels sluggish and needs more time to establish or reverse a bank. Several factors determine roll rate. Aileron design matters first: larger ailerons, greater allowable deflection and more effective aerodynamic shaping generally produce a stronger rolling moment. Some aircraft use differential ailerons or Frise ailerons to improve control feel and reduce adverse yaw, but the core point is that aileron effectiveness directly drives roll response. Wingspan influences roll rate: longer wings increase the rolling moment of inertia and also the roll damping, which reduces how quickly the aircraft accelerates in roll; shorter wings usually allow a faster roll response for the same control power. Airspeed increases aileron effectiveness, because aerodynamic forces scale with dynamic pressure. As airspeed rises, a given aileron deflection produces more force and a higher roll rate, up to the limits where structural loads, compressibility or wing twist reduce or even reverse the effectiveness. Wing dihedral affects lateral stability: dihedral creates a restoring roll moment in a sideslip, which tends to return the aircraft toward wings-level; that stability can slightly oppose rapid roll changes and influences how the aircraft feels during roll inputs. Finally, moment of inertia is a major limiter. Aircraft with mass far from the centreline — long wings, heavy fuel outboard, or wing-tip equipment — have higher roll inertia and respond more slowly to the same aileron input. Two common design features related to ailerons are flaperons and aileron droop. Flaperons combine the flap and aileron functions: the surface can move symmetrically to increase lift like a flap, and differentially to create roll like an aileron. Aileron droop is a programmed symmetrical downward deflection of both ailerons when the flaps are lowered, increasing wing camber and lift for slower approaches while preserving roll-control authority.

pages.t: Adverse yaw: mechanism and countermeasures
pages.on: Infographic: (1) mechanism, (2) Frise ailerons, (3) differential aileron deflection (e.g. 15° down / 30° up), (4) rudder–aileron cross-coupling, (5) roll spoilers.
pages.en: Adverse yaw is the tendency of the aircraft to yaw opposite to the direction of roll when you apply aileron. The mechanism is simple: the down-going aileron increases camber and lift on that wing, but it also increases induced drag and often profile drag. That extra drag pulls the nose toward the wing with the down-going aileron, so during a roll into a turn the nose initially yaws the wrong way unless it is corrected. Designers and pilots use several countermeasures. Frise ailerons create drag on the up-aileron side: when the aileron deflects upward, its nose projects below the wing's lower surface into the airflow, increasing drag on the wing that is losing lift. This added drag helps balance the drag increase on the down-aileron wing, reducing the yaw opposite to the roll. Differential aileron deflection reduces the problem by making the up-going aileron move further than the down-going aileron. Since the down-going aileron is the main source of the extra drag, limiting its travel reduces the drag difference between the wings and therefore the adverse yaw. Rudder–aileron interconnection (cross-coupling) is an automatic solution: a linkage or system applies a small amount of rudder in the direction of the turn whenever the pilot applies aileron. This reduces workload and keeps the aircraft better aligned during roll-in and roll-out, particularly on aircraft with strong adverse-yaw characteristics. Roll spoilers provide roll control by spoiling lift on one wing: instead of relying only on a down-going aileron to increase lift, a spoiler on the down-going (inside) wing deploys to reduce lift there, creating a rolling moment. Because the roll is produced mainly by reducing lift rather than adding lift and induced drag — and the raised spoiler adds drag on the inside wing — roll spoilers reduce adverse yaw, even giving favourable yaw, and remain effective at high speeds where aileron effectiveness may be limited. In practice, even with these design features, pilots still use rudder to fine-tune coordination, keeping the ball centred and the turn smooth.

pages.t: Aircraft roll/yaw interaction
pages.on: Infographic: (1) roll → yaw (adverse yaw), (2) yaw → roll (induced roll toward the yaw; advancing wing generates more lift).
pages.en: Roll and yaw are tightly linked, because changing lift usually changes drag, and yawing changes the relative wind the wings see. That is why pilots treat coordination as a combined roll-and-yaw task, not two separate controls. Roll causing yaw — adverse yaw: when you apply aileron, one aileron goes down and the other goes up. The wing with the down-going aileron produces more lift but also more drag, especially induced drag, and that drag difference pulls the nose opposite to the direction of roll. So if you roll left, the right wing has more drag and the aircraft initially yaws right. Adverse yaw is most noticeable at low speeds and high angles of attack, where induced drag is larger, and the pilot counters it with coordinated rudder so the nose stays aligned with the turn. Yaw causing roll: a yaw disturbance creates a sideslip, meaning the relative wind now comes partly from the side. That changes the effective angle of attack and the airflow distribution across the wings. The advancing wing — the wing on the outside of the yaw — sees a higher effective airflow and, depending on dihedral, sweep and wing position, generates more lift than the other wing. The result is a rolling moment that rolls the aircraft in the direction of the yaw. This is part of the same coupling that produces motions such as Dutch roll and the spiral mode. So the takeaway: rolling inputs create yaw through drag differences, and yaw disturbances create roll by changing the relative wind over the wings. Smooth turns depend on managing both together: aileron sets the bank, and rudder keeps the aircraft aligned and stops the coupling from becoming an unwanted slip, skid or oscillation.
pages.th: Roll และ yaw ผูกกันแน่น เพราะการเปลี่ยนแรงยกมักเปลี่ยนแรงต้าน และการ yaw เปลี่ยนลมสัมพัทธ์ที่ปีกเห็น นักบินจึงถือว่าการประสานเป็นงาน roll และ yaw ร่วมกัน ไม่ใช่สองการบังคับแยกกัน roll ทำให้เกิด yaw คือ adverse yaw เมื่อใช้ aileron ข้างหนึ่งลงอีกข้างขึ้น ปีกที่ aileron ลงมีแรงยกมากขึ้นแต่แรงต้านมากขึ้นด้วย โดยเฉพาะแรงต้านเหนี่ยวนำ ความต่างของแรงต้านดึงหัวไปทางตรงข้ามกับทิศ roll ถ้า roll ซ้าย ปีกขวามีแรงต้านมากกว่า เครื่องจึง yaw ขวาในช่วงแรก adverse yaw เห็นชัดที่สุดที่ความเร็วต่ำและมุมปะทะสูง ซึ่งแรงต้านเหนี่ยวนำมาก นักบินแก้ด้วย rudder ประสานเพื่อให้หัวอยู่ในแนวการเลี้ยว yaw ทำให้เกิด roll การรบกวนแบบ yaw ทำให้เกิด sideslip คือลมสัมพัทธ์มาจากด้านข้างบางส่วน ซึ่งเปลี่ยนมุมปะทะประสิทธิผลและการกระจายกระแสอากาศบนปีก ปีกที่เคลื่อนไปข้างหน้า คือปีกด้านนอกของการ yaw ได้กระแสอากาศประสิทธิผลมากกว่า และขึ้นกับ dihedral, sweep และตำแหน่งปีก สร้างแรงยกมากกว่าอีกปีก ผลคือโมเมนต์ roll ที่ทำให้เครื่อง roll ไปทางเดียวกับการ yaw นี่เป็นส่วนหนึ่งของการจับคู่แบบเดียวกันที่ทำให้เกิดการเคลื่อนที่อย่าง Dutch roll และ spiral mode สรุป การ roll สร้าง yaw ผ่านความต่างของแรงต้าน และการรบกวน yaw สร้าง roll โดยเปลี่ยนลมสัมพัทธ์บนปีก การเลี้ยวที่นุ่มนวลขึ้นกับการจัดการทั้งสองร่วมกัน aileron ตั้งมุมเอียง และ rudder รักษาแนวเครื่อง และกันไม่ให้การจับคู่กลายเป็น slip, skid หรือการแกว่งที่ไม่ต้องการ

pages.t: Aerodynamic balance: benefits for aircraft control and performance
pages.on: Infographic: (1) reduced effort, (2) increased efficiency, (3) enhanced stability; airliner photos.
pages.en: Aerodynamic balance is about designing control surfaces so that the airflow helps the pilot instead of fighting them. The goal is to reduce the hinge moments that create heavy control forces, especially as speed rises. Reduced effort: when a control surface is aerodynamically balanced, the pressures on the surface are arranged so the pilot needs less force to move and hold it. This reduces workload and fatigue, particularly at higher airspeeds where unbalanced control forces can become very heavy, and it makes small, accurate corrections easier without over-controlling. Better control response: with lighter, more consistent forces the pilot can apply smoother inputs, and the surface moves more precisely to the intended deflection. That helps with fine attitude control, coordinated turns and stable approaches, because the aircraft responds predictably to small control changes. Consistent handling: aerodynamic balance also supports consistent control forces across different conditions as speed, configuration and loading change. Balanced controls help maintain a steady feel and reduce sudden changes in control force or sensitivity, so the aircraft stays easier to trim and to keep in equilibrium, whether you are slow on approach, cruising, or manoeuvring. Designers must not over-balance a surface, though: some force must remain so the pilot can feel the load and the controls do not become too light.
pages.th: Aerodynamic balance คือการออกแบบพื้นผิวควบคุมให้กระแสอากาศช่วยนักบินแทนที่จะต้าน เป้าหมายคือลด hinge moment ที่ทำให้แรงที่คันบังคับหนัก โดยเฉพาะเมื่อความเร็วเพิ่ม ลดแรงที่ใช้ เมื่อพื้นผิวควบคุมถูกถ่วงสมดุลทางอากาศพลศาสตร์ ความดันบนพื้นผิวถูกจัดให้นักบินใช้แรงน้อยลงในการขยับและถือไว้ ลดภาระงานและความเหนื่อยล้า โดยเฉพาะที่ความเร็วสูงซึ่งแรงที่ไม่สมดุลอาจหนักมาก และทำให้แก้เล็กน้อยได้แม่นยำโดยไม่บังคับเกิน การตอบสนองดีขึ้น เมื่อแรงเบาและสม่ำเสมอ นักบินบังคับได้นุ่มนวลขึ้น และพื้นผิวเคลื่อนไปยังตำแหน่งที่ตั้งใจได้แม่นยำขึ้น ช่วยการคุมท่าทางละเอียด การเลี้ยวประสาน และ approach ที่นิ่ง เพราะเครื่องตอบสนองการบังคับเล็กน้อยได้อย่างคาดเดาได้ การบังคับที่สม่ำเสมอ aerodynamic balance ยังช่วยให้แรงที่คันบังคับสม่ำเสมอในสภาพต่าง ๆ เมื่อความเร็ว configuration และการบรรทุกเปลี่ยน คันบังคับที่สมดุลช่วยรักษาความรู้สึกที่คงที่และลดการเปลี่ยนแรงหรือความไวอย่างกะทันหัน เครื่องจึง trim และรักษาสมดุลได้ง่าย ไม่ว่าจะช้าตอน approach, cruise หรือหลบหลีก แต่ผู้ออกแบบต้องไม่ถ่วงสมดุลมากเกินไป ต้องเหลือแรงไว้บ้างให้นักบินรู้สึกถึงแรงและคันบังคับไม่เบาเกินไป

pages.t: Nose balance: aerodynamic force reduction technique
pages.on: Infographic: (1) concept — with/without nose balance, (2) mechanism — area ahead of hinge line, (3) real-world rudder horn.
pages.en: Nose balance — the horn balance is one form of it — is a method of aerodynamic balancing in which part of the control surface extends ahead of the hinge line. When the surface deflects, the airflow acts on that forward area and produces a force that helps rotate the surface about the hinge. In effect, the balance area produces an assisting moment that reduces the hinge moment the pilot or actuator has to overcome. The result is lighter control forces, smoother feel and better controllability, especially as airspeed increases and aerodynamic loads get larger. You commonly see horn balances on rudders and elevators, where designers want enough authority without excessively heavy pedal or control-column forces.
pages.th: Nose balance (horn balance เป็นรูปแบบหนึ่ง) เป็นวิธีถ่วงสมดุลทางอากาศพลศาสตร์ที่ส่วนหนึ่งของพื้นผิวควบคุมยื่นไปหน้าเส้นบานพับ เมื่อพื้นผิวโยก กระแสอากาศกระทำบนพื้นที่ด้านหน้านั้นและสร้างแรงที่ช่วยหมุนพื้นผิวรอบบานพับ พื้นที่ถ่วงสมดุลจึงสร้างโมเมนต์ช่วยที่ลด hinge moment ที่นักบินหรือ actuator ต้องเอาชนะ ผลคือแรงที่คันบังคับเบาลง ความรู้สึกนุ่มขึ้น และควบคุมได้ดีขึ้น โดยเฉพาะเมื่อความเร็วเพิ่มและแรงอากาศพลศาสตร์มากขึ้น มักเห็น horn balance ที่ rudder และ elevator ซึ่งผู้ออกแบบต้องการอำนาจควบคุมเพียงพอโดยไม่ให้แรงที่แป้นหรือคันบังคับหนักเกินไป

pages.t: Internal balance: reducing pilot control force
pages.on: Infographic: "internal weights (e.g. lead) shift the control-surface CG forward" — this is mass balance, not internal balance.
pages.en: Internal balance is a form of aerodynamic balance in which the nose of the control surface, ahead of the hinge, is extended into a sealed chamber inside the rear of the wing or tailplane. A flexible seal connects the balance panel to the fixed structure. When the surface is deflected, the pressure difference between the upper and lower surfaces of the wing acts on the balance panel inside the chamber and produces a moment that helps move the control surface. The result is lighter, smoother control forces without any part of the surface protruding into the airflow, so it adds little drag. Be careful not to confuse this with mass balance: weights placed inside the surface ahead of the hinge move the control surface's centre of gravity forward. That does not reduce aerodynamic hinge moments in steady flight; its purpose is to prevent control-surface flutter by stopping the surface from lagging or oscillating, as covered in the flutter lesson.
pages.th: Internal balance เป็นการถ่วงสมดุลทางอากาศพลศาสตร์รูปแบบหนึ่ง ส่วนหน้าของพื้นผิวควบคุม ซึ่งอยู่หน้าบานพับ ยื่นเข้าไปในช่องปิดผนึกในส่วนหลังของปีกหรือแพนหางระดับ มีแผ่นซีลแบบยืดหยุ่นเชื่อมแผ่นถ่วงสมดุลกับโครงสร้างที่อยู่กับที่ เมื่อพื้นผิวโยก ความต่างความดันระหว่างผิวบนและผิวล่างของปีกกระทำบนแผ่นถ่วงสมดุลในช่องนั้น และสร้างโมเมนต์ที่ช่วยขยับพื้นผิวควบคุม ผลคือแรงที่คันบังคับเบาและนุ่มขึ้น โดยไม่มีส่วนใดของพื้นผิวยื่นออกไปในกระแสอากาศ จึงเพิ่มแรงต้านน้อย ระวังอย่าสับสนกับ mass balance ตุ้มน้ำหนักที่วางในพื้นผิวหน้าบานพับจะย้าย CG ของพื้นผิวควบคุมไปข้างหน้า ซึ่งไม่ได้ลด hinge moment ทางอากาศพลศาสตร์ในการบินคงที่ จุดประสงค์คือป้องกัน flutter ของพื้นผิวควบคุม โดยไม่ให้พื้นผิวเคลื่อนตามช้าหรือสั่น ตามที่เรียนในบท flutter

pages.t: Types of aircraft control tabs
pages.on: Infographic: (1) balance tab, (2) anti-balance tab, (3) spring tab, (4) servo tab ("connected directly to a servo motor … autopilots or fly-by-wire").
pages.en: Tabs are small auxiliary surfaces at the trailing edge of a primary control surface, used to change control forces and handling feel. Here is how the main types work. Balance tab: a balance tab is geared to deflect opposite to the main surface, creating an aerodynamic force that helps move the main control surface. Its purpose is to reduce the control force — the hinge moment — making the surface easier to deflect, especially at higher speeds. Anti-balance tab: an anti-balance (anti-servo) tab moves in the same direction as the main surface, producing a force that resists the surface movement. This increases control feel and helps prevent over-controlling, which is why it is used where the controls would otherwise be too light — typically on all-flying tails (stabilators). Spring tab: in a spring tab the tab is connected through a spring, so its deflection depends on the force the pilot applies rather than directly on the control position. At low speed the spring hardly deflects and the tab has little effect; at higher speed the aerodynamic load increases and the tab gives more assistance, so the pilot's force rises less steeply with speed. Servo tab: a servo tab is arranged so that the pilot's controls move only the tab, and the tab's aerodynamic force moves the main control surface. This is useful when the main surface is large or heavily loaded, because the tab provides a lot of control power for relatively little pilot effort. On some aircraft tabs can also be adjusted to provide trim.
pages.th: Tab เป็นพื้นผิวช่วยขนาดเล็กที่ชายหลังของพื้นผิวควบคุมหลัก ใช้เปลี่ยนแรงที่คันบังคับและความรู้สึกการบังคับ ชนิดหลักทำงานดังนี้ Balance tab ต่อกลไกให้โยกตรงข้ามกับพื้นผิวหลัก สร้างแรงอากาศพลศาสตร์ที่ช่วยขยับพื้นผิวควบคุมหลัก จุดประสงค์คือลดแรงที่คันบังคับ คือ hinge moment ทำให้โยกพื้นผิวง่ายขึ้น โดยเฉพาะที่ความเร็วสูง Anti-balance tab (anti-servo tab) เคลื่อนไปทิศเดียวกับพื้นผิวหลัก สร้างแรงที่ต้านการเคลื่อนของพื้นผิว เพิ่มความรู้สึกที่คันบังคับและช่วยกันการบังคับเกิน จึงใช้ในที่ที่คันบังคับจะเบาเกินไป โดยทั่วไปคือหางแบบ all-flying (stabilator) Spring tab tab เชื่อมผ่านสปริง การโยกของมันจึงขึ้นกับแรงที่นักบินใช้ แทนที่จะขึ้นกับตำแหน่งคันบังคับโดยตรง ที่ความเร็วต่ำสปริงแทบไม่ยืด tab จึงมีผลน้อย ที่ความเร็วสูงแรงอากาศพลศาสตร์มากขึ้นและ tab ช่วยมากขึ้น แรงของนักบินจึงเพิ่มตามความเร็วน้อยลง Servo tab จัดให้คันบังคับของนักบินขยับเฉพาะ tab และแรงอากาศพลศาสตร์ของ tab เป็นตัวขยับพื้นผิวควบคุมหลัก มีประโยชน์เมื่อพื้นผิวหลักใหญ่หรือรับแรงมาก เพราะ tab ให้กำลังควบคุมมากโดยนักบินใช้แรงค่อนข้างน้อย ในบางเครื่อง tab ยังปรับเพื่อ trim ได้ด้วย
pages.kEn: Balance: opposite, lighter. Anti-balance: same way, heavier. Spring: assists more as speed rises. Servo: pilot moves tab, tab moves surface.

pages.t: Balance tab: aerodynamic assist for control surfaces
pages.on: Infographic: (1) small tab on trailing edge, (2) moves opposite to the main surface, (3) tab force assists movement; real-world elevator photo ("[cite: 132]").
pages.en: A balance tab is a small tab on the trailing edge of a primary control surface, such as an elevator or rudder. When the main control surface deflects, the balance tab moves in the opposite direction through a fixed linkage. That opposite movement creates an aerodynamic force on the tab, which produces a moment about the hinge line. The moment from the tab assists the movement of the main surface, reducing the hinge moment the pilot has to overcome. In practical terms, a balance tab makes the controls lighter and helps the pilot achieve the same surface deflection with less force, especially at higher airspeeds where the aerodynamic loads are greater. The price is a small loss of control effectiveness, because the tab force acts against the surface's own aerodynamic force.
pages.th: Balance tab เป็น tab เล็กบนชายหลังของพื้นผิวควบคุมหลัก เช่น elevator หรือ rudder เมื่อพื้นผิวควบคุมหลักโยก balance tab จะเคลื่อนไปทิศตรงข้ามผ่านกลไกเชื่อมตายตัว การเคลื่อนตรงข้ามนั้นสร้างแรงอากาศพลศาสตร์บน tab ซึ่งสร้างโมเมนต์รอบเส้นบานพับ โมเมนต์จาก tab ช่วยการเคลื่อนของพื้นผิวหลัก ลด hinge moment ที่นักบินต้องเอาชนะ ในทางปฏิบัติ balance tab ทำให้คันบังคับเบาลง และช่วยให้นักบินโยกพื้นผิวได้เท่าเดิมด้วยแรงที่น้อยลง โดยเฉพาะที่ความเร็วสูงซึ่งแรงอากาศพลศาสตร์มากกว่า สิ่งที่ต้องแลกคือประสิทธิผลการควบคุมลดลงเล็กน้อย เพราะแรงที่ tab กระทำสวนกับแรงอากาศพลศาสตร์ของพื้นผิวเอง

pages.kTh: Balance tab: ต่อกลไก สวนทางพื้นผิว → แรงเบาลง ประสิทธิผลลดเล็กน้อย

pages.t: Anti-balance tab: aerodynamic load addition for control feel
pages.on: Infographic: (1) tab adds hinge moment, (2) moves in the same direction as the surface, (3) adds load and feel; real-world stabilator photo ("[cite: 133]").
pages.en: An anti-balance tab works by adding aerodynamic hinge moment instead of cancelling it. The tab is mounted on the trailing edge of the main control surface — most commonly an all-flying tail (stabilator). When the control surface moves, the anti-balance tab moves in the same direction. Because it deflects the same way, the airflow on the tab creates a force that produces a hinge moment opposing the pilot's input. The result: the pilot must apply more control force to achieve the same surface deflection. What does it do? One, it provides control feel — artificial heaviness. A stabilator pivots near its aerodynamic centre, so without the tab it could feel far too light and sensitive; the anti-balance tab increases the control forces and gives the pilot better tactile feedback. Two, it reduces the risk of over-control and pilot-induced oscillation (PIO). By making the controls heavier, it discourages abrupt or excessive inputs, which is especially important at high speed, where small deflections can create large pitch changes. Three, it improves handling at high speed: the aircraft feels less twitchy in pitch, making it easier to hold attitude precisely in cruise and during manoeuvring. So balance tabs lighten the controls, while anti-balance tabs deliberately add load to improve feel and prevent over-controlling.
pages.th: Anti-balance tab ทำงานโดยเพิ่ม hinge moment ทางอากาศพลศาสตร์แทนที่จะหักล้าง tab ติดที่ชายหลังของพื้นผิวควบคุมหลัก ส่วนใหญ่คือหางแบบ all-flying (stabilator) เมื่อพื้นผิวควบคุมเคลื่อน anti-balance tab จะเคลื่อนไปทิศเดียวกัน เพราะโยกไปทางเดียวกัน กระแสอากาศบน tab จึงสร้างแรงที่ทำให้เกิด hinge moment ต้านการบังคับของนักบิน ผลคือนักบินต้องออกแรงมากขึ้นเพื่อโยกพื้นผิวเท่าเดิม หน้าที่มีดังนี้ หนึ่ง ให้ความรู้สึกที่คันบังคับ คือความหนักเทียม stabilator หมุนรอบจุดใกล้ศูนย์อากาศพลศาสตร์ของมัน ถ้าไม่มี tab อาจรู้สึกเบาและไวเกินไปมาก anti-balance tab เพิ่มแรงที่คันบังคับและให้นักบินรู้สึกได้ดีขึ้น สอง ลดความเสี่ยงการบังคับเกินและ pilot-induced oscillation (PIO) การทำให้คันบังคับหนักขึ้นช่วยกันการบังคับกระชากหรือมากเกินไป ซึ่งสำคัญมากที่ความเร็วสูง ที่การโยกเล็กน้อยทำให้ pitch เปลี่ยนมาก สาม การบังคับที่ความเร็วสูงดีขึ้น เครื่องรู้สึกไม่ไวเกินใน pitch รักษาท่าทางได้แม่นยำขึ้นตอน cruise และหลบหลีก สรุป balance tab ทำให้คันบังคับเบาลง ส่วน anti-balance tab ตั้งใจเพิ่มแรงเพื่อความรู้สึกที่ดีขึ้นและกันการบังคับเกิน

pages.t: Spring tab: control feel via spring-loaded assistance
pages.on: Infographic: (1) tab with spring in the linkage, (2) force-dependent movement, (3) consistent feel and controllability ("[cite: 135]").
pages.en: A spring tab is a small tab on the trailing edge of a main control surface, often the elevator. Unlike a simple balance tab, which moves purely by fixed linkage, a spring tab's movement depends on the control force, because a spring is built into the linkage. When the pilot moves the control, the linkage tries to move the main surface, but the aerodynamic load resists it. That resistance compresses or stretches the spring, which allows the tab to deflect. The deflected tab creates an aerodynamic force that helps drive the main surface in the commanded direction. At low speed the aerodynamic loads are small, so the spring hardly winds up and the tab effect is minimal — the controls work almost as if there were no tab. At high speed the aerodynamic loads are larger, the spring deflects more, and the tab gives more assistance, acting increasingly like a balance tab. What does it do? One, it keeps the control feel more consistent across the speed range. As airspeed increases, control forces would normally rise steeply; the spring tab increases its assistance with speed, so the pilot's required force stays more consistent and manageable. Two, it improves controllability at high speed, where the main surface would otherwise be heavy: the tab gives aerodynamic help so the pilot can still make precise pitch changes without excessive force. Three, it reduces pilot workload and helps prevent over-control: because the force gradient can be tailored, the aircraft feels steadier, which supports smoother handling and reduces the chance of pilot-induced oscillation. In short, a spring tab uses a spring-loaded linkage, so the tab becomes more active as the aerodynamic loads rise, giving controlled assistance and a more uniform control feel across the speed range.

pages.t: Servo tab: power-assisted control via aerodynamic force
pages.on: Infographic: (1) pilot moves the tab, not the surface, (2) airflow as the power source, (3) reduced effort; real-world rudder servo-tab linkage ("[cite: 138]").
pages.en: A servo tab is a small tab on the trailing edge of a main control surface, often a rudder or elevator. The key difference is that the pilot moves only the tab, not the main surface directly; the main surface is free to float on its hinge. The pilot's control input deflects the servo tab. Airflow over the deflected tab creates an aerodynamic force on it, and because the tab is attached to the main surface, that force produces a hinge moment that drives the main surface in the desired direction — opposite to the tab. As the main surface moves, the system reaches a new balance where the aerodynamic moments of the tab and the main surface match the pilot's commanded position. So the tab uses the airflow as the power source to move the larger surface. What does it do? One, it reduces pilot effort dramatically: since the pilot is only moving a small tab, control forces stay light even when the main surface is large or heavily loaded. Two, it makes large control surfaces practical: on aircraft with big rudders or elevators and high aerodynamic loads, a direct mechanical system could be too heavy to operate, and servo tabs allow effective control without hydraulic boost. Three, it keeps the aircraft controllable across a wide speed range, because the tab's force grows with speed. The limitation is at low speed: with little dynamic pressure the tab produces little force, so the control response is sluggish. In short, the pilot commands the tab, the airflow supplies the force, and that force moves the main control surface, giving power-assisted control without a powered actuator.

numbers: Pitching moment = tail force × tail arm; low speed → tail download, large up-elevator.
Forward CG: larger nose-down moment, longer tail arm, more elevator needed, higher stall speed (POH stall speeds at forward CG). Aft CG: less stability, lighter forces.
Control check: yoke LEFT → LEFT aileron UP. Bank toward the up-aileron.
Adverse yaw: roll left → right aileron down → right-wing drag → nose yaws right. Fixes: Frise, differential, interconnect, roll spoilers (spoiler up on the down-going wing).
Tabs: balance = opposite, lighter; anti-balance = same direction, heavier (stabilators); spring = more assistance with speed; servo = pilot moves tab only.
C172S max demonstrated crosswind 15 kt (POH). DA42 engine-out: 2–5° bank toward live engine (AFM — SME).
